Using survey data, we document a substantial dispersion in artificial intelligence (AI) pessimism that is negatively correlated with worker income. Motivated by these findings, we build a dynamic Mirrlees income taxation model with ambiguity-averse workers. Workers form endogenous worst-case beliefs about the impact of new technologies, that vary by skill level. This endogenous heterogeneity in expectations enables the formulation of government policies that indirectly influence workers’ subjective beliefs to enhance welfare. We calibrate the model to the empirical findings on AI expectations and solve for optimal tax schedules and AI investment. We find that uncertainty over AI motivates a more progressive labor income tax schedule, combined with a mostly flat savings subsidy of about 12%. The optimal policy reverses the sign of the empirical relationship between AI pessimism and worker income.

Session 6B: Family, Education and Household Production

Parenting Style and Fertility: A Cross-country Analysis
Siew Ling Yew (Monash University); with Shuyun May Li, Solmaz Moslehi, Yao Yao
Session 6B · Sun 22 Nov, 09:30–10:00 · Room B

Parenting style and fertility are inherently interrelated. Intensive parenting increases parental effort and discourages fertility, while having more children constrains the time and effort parents can devote to each child, shaping parenting choices. Despite this interaction, existing research has largely studied fertility and parenting style in isolation. This paper bridges the two literatures by examining how socioeconomic conditions and policies jointly shape parents’ choices of fertility and parenting style, and how parenting style mediates fertility outcomes. Using data from the World Values Survey, we document systematic cross-country patterns in parenting styles and fertility across stages of economic development. As income rises, parenting shifts from authoritarian to authoritative and eventually toward permissive styles, while fertility declines and partially rebounds in high-income economies. Micro-level evidence confirms that, relative to authoritative parents, authoritarian parents have more children, whereas permissive parents have fewer. To interpret these patterns, we develop a quantitative overlapping-generations model in which parents jointly choose fertility and parenting style in response to socioeconomic environments, including returns to education, inequality, structural change, and the marketisation of childcare. The model is calibrated to a benchmark economy, US, and to a selective group of countries at different development stages to account for observed patterns in fertility and parenting style within and across countries. Our quantitative analysis aims to uncover the role of parenting style in the quantity–quality tradeoff underlying fertility decisions, evaluates the contribution of socioeconomic and macro factors, and assesses policies aimed at raising fertility.

College as Human Capital Investment or Tournament: A Macroeconomic Analysis
Siyu Shi (New York University Abu Dhabi)
Session 6B · Sun 22 Nov, 10:00–10:30 · Room B

A college education is commonly viewed as a productive investment, but it also serves a competitive purpose by allowing individuals to stand out in the job market, as in a tournament. I study the relative importance of these two channels in determining college attendance. I build a general equilibrium life-cycle model with a college decision, human capital investments, and skill allocation. The model’s novelty is that workers are allocated to different occupations based on their relative ranking of accumulated human capital, so a college education also has competitive value. Parameterizing the model to the U.S. economy, I find that the competitive channel accounts for 27% of college attendance but encourages overinvestment in human capital accumulation. The optimal policy lowers college subsidies and tax progressivity, improving welfare by 0.9% by mitigating competition in college education and its negative externalities. The results are also robust when subsidies are reformed to be wealth- or merit-based.

Saving by Shopping? The Limits of Substitution in Household Production
Kozo Ueda (Waseda University); with Miyu Iwasaki
Session 6B · Sun 22 Nov, 10:30–11:00 · Room B

To what extent can households buffer cost-of-living shocks by shopping more efficiently? Using novel retailer scanner data linked to individual shoppers at a single supermarket, we isolate the savings generated by the intensive margin of shopping. We develop a structural model of endogenous shopping frequency and estimate the elasticity of substitution between time and market goods implied by this intensive margin to be approximately 0.3, which is well below the values exceeding unity typically assumed in macroeconomics. This suggests that the within-store timing margin alone affords households only limited scope to smooth consumption through shopping effort. Welfare analysis shows that increases in fixed time costs lead to sizable welfare losses.

Session 6C: Housing Finance and Mortgages

Tenancy Without Rent, Credit Without Banks: Housing as Repo in Korea
Yunho Cho (Sogang University); with Yoonsoo Lee, Hyeonuk Shin
Session 6C · Sun 22 Nov, 09:30–10:00 · Room C

This paper studies a housing finance system in which tenants provide credit directly to landlords. In Korea, this arrangement is known as jeonse. Tenants transfer a large refundable deposit in place of rent, allowing landlords to finance housing investment with tenant funds. To quantify the implications of jeonse, we develop a general equilibrium heterogeneous-agent life-cycle model in which households choose among homeownership, jeonse, and periodic rent. The model features subjective beliefs about future house prices, which governs expected capital gains and landlords’ willingness to supply jeonse housing. We calibrate the model to Korean micro-data and discipline this belief using observed rates of jeonse and rental supply. The model shows that deposit financing alone cannot sustain jeonse without sufficiently optimistic price beliefs. Eliminating jeonse reduces deposit-financed housing investment but redirects tenants toward homeownership and periodic rent. The reallocation effect dominates, raising house prices by 15.8% and rents by 18.8%. Relaxing jeonse loan limits expands young households’ access to jeonse and later homeownership, but also increases landlord financing and raises prices and rents. Jeonse therefore expands housing access while providing belief-driven leverage to housing investors.

Competition, risk, and pricing in the US Mortgage Market
Mei Dong (University of Melbourne); with Eungwon Lee, May Li
Session 6C · Sun 22 Nov, 10:00–10:30 · Room C

We study how banking competition affects mortgage pricing in the mortgage market. Using the US mortgage data from 2014 to 2019, we find that greater competition in the local mortgage market is associated with higher mortgage rates and riskier borrower pools. These relationships are nonlinear: both effects are stronger in markets that are more competitive. Moreover, regions in which borrower risk responds more to competition exhibit larger increases in mortgage rates. We develop a model where lenders choose both loan supply and loan risk while engaging in Cournot competition in loan and funding markets. Competition lowers the loan rate through the conventional Cournot channel but also induces greater risk-taking. When competition is sufficiently intense, the risk effect dominates the Cournot effect, so further competition raises rather than lowers mortgage rates. These results highlight a risk-taking channel through which greater banking competition can increase borrowing costs.

The Political Economy of Government Mortgage Guarantees
Jiheum Yeon (Korea Institute for International Economic Policy); with Dong Ho Kang
Session 6C · Sun 22 Nov, 10:30–11:00 · Room C

Government insurance of mortgage credit risk has survived decades of reform, even though normative analyses find that it lowers aggregate welfare. To understand why the policy that is realized diverges from the policy that is optimal, we develop a quantitative housing model in which the guarantee fee is selected by a political criterion. The economy is populated by groups with opposing stakes in mortgage policy and different degrees of patience: impatient borrowers, who finance housing with defaultable long-term mortgages and choose between owning and renting, and patient savers and landlords. Raising the fee is passed through to the mortgage rate, lowers house prices and the housing stock, and redistributes permanently from borrowers to savers and landlords. Whether the fee is raised therefore depends on the horizon over which each group’s stake is capitalized. A planner who values claims over an infinite horizon adopts the highest admissible fee, whereas a policymaker accountable over any empirically relevant horizon retains the low fee: the horizon at which the two criteria agree is roughly 27 years, an order of magnitude longer than an electoral term. The subsidy persists not because it is efficient, but because those who would lose from its removal are impatient and hold a large stake.

Session 6D: Market Power and Production Networks

Fixed Costs, Product Heterogeneity, and The Force of Competition
Maria Ptashkina (University of Melbourne); with Vladimir Asriyan, Alberto Martin, Jaume Ventura
Session 6D · Sun 22 Nov, 09:30–10:00 · Room D

One of the most remarkable facts of the US economy over the last few decades is the rise of fixed costs. Indeed, the fixed-cost share (ratio of fixed to total costs) of the US economy has increased significantly during this period, as has its dispersion across firms. This paper provides a framework to think about the macroeconomic origin and effects of fixed costs. The core of the framework is that goods are heterogeneous, as they differ in their demand elasticities, as well as in their fixed and variable costs. We show that, in a contestable equilibrium, the economy’s fixed-costs share is determined endogenously both by the extensive margin, i.e., the set of goods being produced, and the intensive margin, i.e., the quantity produced of each good. These two margins also shape the effects of economic growth in the fixed-cost share: while intensive growth tends to reduce the fixedcost share by raising the number of units produced, extensive growth tends to increase the fixed-cost share by activating goods with increasingly high fixed-costs. We use a numerical exploration of the model to rationalize the evolution of fixed costs in the US, and perform a normative analysis of the fixed-cost economy to characterize the distortions that affect the intensive and extensive margins of production in the contestable equilibrium.

Propagation over Production Networks with Endogenous Market Power
Daniel Prosi (New York University Abu Dhabi)
Session 6D · Sun 22 Nov, 10:00–10:30 · Room D

This paper studies how changes to firm productivity or size propagate over a production network. It derives an endogenous measure of market power when firms internalise their position in the production network to extract monopoly rents. The paper first explores the relation between network position and endogenous markups under general non-parametric production functions. This separates economically meaningful channels of interaction from restrictions introduced by the choice of functional form of production and the competition regime. It then studies how changes to productivity or firm-size propagate over the network when markups are endogenous. The forward equation of productivity gains and the backward equation of demand creation are complemented with a horizontal equation that captures changes in endogenous market power. Using granular administrative data from Rwanda and an instrumental variable strategy based on exogenous border closures, the paper tests the empirical validity of the derived measures. It then uses the universe of firm-to-firm interactions in the country to study the network-position of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in Rwanda and assess the general equilibrium effects of FDI on the domestic economy via efficiency gains, demand creation, and changes to the structure of competition.

Self-Fulfilling Sentiment(s) in Production Networks
Weimin Zhou (Sichuan University); with Renbin Zhang, Jinhui Xu, Zijian Wang
Session 6D · Sun 22 Nov, 10:30–11:00 · Room D

Building on the sentiment mechanism of Benhabib et al. (2015), we study self-fulfilling price movements in a production network. Firms set prices using noisy signals that confound local costs with endogenous prices, while supplier prices enter buyers’ marginal costs. Production links therefore create an additional feedback channel through which belief-induced price responses can be inferred and retransmitted. For aggregate sentiment, production links enable a self-fulfilling price movement when firms’ common-price exposure is sufficiently aligned with their input-sourcing patterns. We then consider coexisting sectoral sentiments. With local price signals, sentiment must begin in a sector with direct support; supplier-price feedback can then transmit it downstream and allow additional sectors to sustain distinct sentiment movements. With cross-sector price signals, price comovement can provide support even when no sector sustains sentiment alone. Production links and firms’ information thus jointly determine the existence, spread, and dimensionality of sentiment.

Session 7A: New Keynesian and HANK Models

New Keynesian Economics through the Extensive Margin
Akira Ishide (The University of Tokyo); with Saki Bigio
Session 7A · Sun 22 Nov, 11:15–11:45 · Room A

This paper reformulates the New Keynesian model to incorporate output adjustments through the extensive margin. Shifting from adjustments through the intensive to the extensive employment margin, the model introduces predetermined output, altering key properties of the New Keynesian framework. First, the Taylor principle is inverted: stability is achieved when nominal rates respond less than one-for-one with inflation. Second, the model significantly alters the output responses to changes in monetary policy. We argue that this represents a challenge and an opportunity for the literature. Sticky information allows the model to correct the sign of impulse responses.

Zero liquidity and concentrated redistribution in a New Keynesian model
Yuichiro Waki (Aoyama Gakuin University)
Session 7A · Sun 22 Nov, 11:45–12:15 · Room A

The zero-liquidity assumption — households cannot borrow and assets are in zero net supply — simplifies heterogeneous-agent models by eliminating the asset distribution as an aggregate state. I show that it creates a peculiar response to concentrated redistribution in a New Keynesian model. A transfer Δ\Delta distributed among a fraction ε\varepsilon of households reduces period-0 output by Δ/ε\Delta/\varepsilon. Thus, output can remain depressed as Δ\Delta vanishes and can approach zero. If a positive fraction of transfer-paying households can borrow and their constraints are locally slack, the output loss vanishes with Δ\Delta. This fragility warrants caution in highly concentrated transfer experiments.

Learning about monetary policy in Tractable HANK
Christopher Gibbs (University of Sydney); with Paul Kitney, Nigel McClung
Session 7A · Sun 22 Nov, 12:15–12:45 · Room A

A growing literature distils the aggregate properties of Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) models into parsimonious representations with the same reduced form as a Representative Agent New Keynesian (RANK) model. The monetary policy settings that induce determinate and learnable equilibrium in the latter are well-known. We revisit these findings for tractable versions of HANK models. We find that when HANK economies imply countercyclical income risk, their tractable counterparts require different monetary policy settings in order to ensure determinacy and learnability (E-stability) compared to the RANK benchmark. This includes equilibria that are indeterminate and E-stable, while the conventional Taylor principle is satisfied. Monetary policy must be history dependent or place more weight on output stabilization to match the RANK model’s properties.

Session 7B: Social Insurance and Welfare

Public and Self Insurance in Job Search and Consumption: Evidence from Bank Transaction Data
W. Similan Rujiwattanapong (Waseda University); with Fei Gao, Kozo Ueda
Session 7B · Sun 22 Nov, 11:15–11:45 · Room B

How do private savings and public unemployment insurance (UI) interact in shaping job transitions? This paper examines the effects of UI and private wealth on reemployment wages and consumption using novel bank transaction data covering 65,697 individuals in Japan. We develop a job-search model in which unemployed workers choose target wages and consumption while facing UI benefits and financial buffers. The model predicts that UI raises target wages, whereas the effect of wealth is theoretically ambiguous. Empirically, both UI generosity and wealth are associated with higher reemployment wages, and the effect of UI remains strong even among wealthy individuals. Consumption rises with reemployment wages and falls following job separation, particularly for individuals with limited liquidity. UI benefits substantially mitigate these consumption losses and help sustain consumption during nonemployment. Moreover, by increasing reemployment wages, UI continues to affect consumption after reemployment. The results suggest that private wealth and UI play distinct roles in shaping labor market behavior and consumption dynamics and highlight the importance of liquidity constraints in evaluating unemployment insurance policies.

Disability Benefit Reform, Employment and Welfare: Evidence from Australia’s Welfare-to-work Reforms
Man Hin Chio (Australian National University); with Chung Tran
Session 7B · Sun 22 Nov, 11:45–12:15 · Room B

We study the labour market effects of tightening eligibility for disability support among people with partial work capacity. Australia’s 2005 Welfare-to-Work reform lowered the Disability Support Pension (DSP) work capacity threshold from 30 to 15 hours per week, and grandfathering and delayed reassessment generated staggered exposure to the new rule. Using linked administrative records from the Person-Level Integrated Data Asset and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that labour earnings decline upon first exposure and that employment falls in subsequent quarters, with both effects persisting over time. We interpret this evidence using a lifecycle model of the Australian economy that features incomplete markets, saving, discrete labour supply, separate productivity and disability shocks, progressive income taxation, the means-tested Age Pension, and a means-tested DSP with an hours rule, income and assets tests, permanent assessed medical eligibility, and an endogenous claiming decision. Lowering the hours threshold from 30 to 15 in the calibrated model reduces average labour income, hours, and employment in the working-age population, and entrant welfare falls in every education and disability group. A simulation of 100,000 lifecycle paths reproduces the qualitative pattern of the empirical estimates for recipients who remain on and who exit the payment. Our findings suggest that policies targeting eligibility tightening can weaken insurance and generate labour market disincentive effects, reducing employment and earnings instead of promoting work among people with partial work capacity.

Redistribution, distortions, and the welfare effects of Social Security
Ponpoje Porapakkarm (National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies); with Svetlana Pashchenko, Youngsoo Jang
Session 7B · Sun 22 Nov, 12:15–12:45 · Room B

What is the best way to reform Social Security? Academic literature offers diverging advice. There is a well-known result that the optimal size of Social Security is zero, implying it is best to phase the program out. Other studies argue that much can be gained by redesigning the program, given its current size. We provide a unified analysis that examines how the optimal size of Social Security depends on the key features of its design. We first develop a theoretical decomposition tracing the program’s welfare effects to (i) income redistribution, (ii) distortions on the annuitization level, and (iii) intertemporal distortions. We then quantitatively assess the role of these channels. We show that the zero-optimal-size result arises because Social Security is too distortive and not redistributive enough. Once these design flaws are corrected, it is even optimal to increase the size of the program.

Session 7C: Housing Markets and Wealth

Intergenerational Spillovers: The Impact of Labor Market Risk on the Housing Market
Leanne Nam (Aarhus University)
Session 7C · Sun 22 Nov, 11:15–11:45 · Room C

Unemployment leads to large and persistent income losses for workers. Higher unemployment in the labor market therefore has spillover effects on the housing market. This paper studies such spillover effects from both empirical and theoretical perspectives. Using data from the Current Population Survey (CPS), I show that a 1 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate leads to a 1.55% decline in housing prices. Theoretically, I develop an overlapping generations model with a housing market. The calibrated model replicates the empirically observed spillover effect for the U.S. economy. Higher income uncertainty is the main driver of the spillover effect, rather than actual income losses. The spillover effect transmits one-third of the welfare losses of workers due to higher unemployment in the labor market to older, retired households by reducing their housing wealth. Younger workers benefit in part by buying houses at depressed prices. The magnitude of the spillover effect is shaped by the demographic structure of the population and the specific age groups affected by unemployment shocks. I find that increasing the generosity of unemployment insurance stabilizes the housing market, although it only partially mitigates the spillover effect.

Blame the Boomers or Foreigners? A Structural Decomposition of Housing Costs and Intergenerational Inequality.
Takeki Sunakawa (ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office); with Tina Kao, Timothy Kam
Session 7C · Sun 22 Nov, 11:45–12:15 · Room C

We decompose and quantify the different drivers of the cost of home-ownership. We show that immigration accounts for a small share, and this depends on the distribution of immigrant types.

Beyond the Floodplain: Uncovering the Spatial Spillovers of Land Price Declines after Typhoon Hagibis
Fumitaka Nakamura (Bank of Japan); with Toshitaka Maruyama, Hiroaki Shirai, Nao Sudo
Session 7C · Sun 22 Nov, 12:15–12:45 · Room C

We examine how changes in flood-risk perception influence land prices by analyzing price developments in inundated and nearby areas following Typhoon Hagibis (2019), using parcel-level data, inundation maps, and an event-study approach. Our key findings indicate that land prices in inundated areas declined monotonically after the flood, falling 10% after five years. Furthermore, a distance-decay effect is observed, with non-inundated plots within 100 meters of the flood boundary declining by 5%, whereas effects disappear beyond 800 meters. Price declines differ inside and outside official hazard zones, with larger spillover effects in unaffected areas outside the zones. To clarify the mechanism, we extend the Bayesian belief-updating framework of Bakkensen and Barrage (2022) to account for variations in flood-risk perception arising from temporal lags, proximity to the affected area, and hazard-zone designation. Simulation results based on the model show that three factors explain price changes: delayed adjustment of risk perceptions after the flood, reduced impact of flood risk perceptions with distance from the disaster area, and pre-flood incorporation of flood risk into prices within hazard map zones.

Session 7D: Firm Dynamics, Investment and Aggregation

Equilibrium Indeterminacy When Only Some Firms Are Scalable
Oscar Pavlov (University of Tasmania); with Mark Weder
Session 7D · Sun 22 Nov, 11:15–11:45 · Room D

This paper develops a dynamic general equilibrium model with heterogeneous firm scalability and studies its implications for macroeconomic fluctuations. Firms with scalable production technologies endogenously account for a disproportionate share of output, employment, and market power, causing aggregate returns to scale to vary endogenously with macroeconomic activity. We show that empirically plausible differences in firm scalability are sufficient to generate equilibrium indeterminacy. The calibrated model reproduces key features of the U.S. distributions of firm size and markups, while Bayesian estimation indicates both the importance of scale heterogeneity and that animal spirits shocks account for a non-negligible share of business cycle fluctuations, particularly in investment.

Lumpy Investment Commitments and Smooth Capital Expenditure
Ikuo Takei (Asia School of Business); with Ryota Ogaki
Session 7D · Sun 22 Nov, 11:45–12:15 · Room D

Using mandatory project-level disclosures by Japanese listed firms, we observe multi-year in- vestment commitments separately from capital expenditure. Commitments are lumpy: in most firm-years firms start no new project, and a firm’s largest year carries most of its commitments. Capital expenditure is smooth, because each commitment is paid out over a multi-year build. Commitments also respond about twice as strongly as spending to cash flow and to analysts’ sales-forecast revisions, mostly through new projects. A calibrated investment-planning model with a single pipeline state attributes both gaps to time to build, not financing constraints, so spending-based measures understate investment responses.

Common Revisions, Relative Positions, and the Micro-Macro Wedge
Greta Meggiorini (University of Auckland)
Session 7D · Sun 22 Nov, 12:15–12:45 · Room D

Forecast-error-on-revision regressions suggest that consensus forecasts underreact while individual forecasts overreact. Using aligned SPF samples, I show that this contrast is unstable across variables, horizons, and sample windows. I derive an exact decomposition of the pooled individual coefficient into slopes on common revisions and changes in forecasters’ positions relative to consensus, weighted by revision synchronization. The common slope is regime-sensitive. The relative-position slope is more stable and negative, but stable relative-position dispersion mechanically implies a benchmark of -1/2, which most output and price estimates do not reject. The individual coefficient is therefore not a standalone test of behavioral bias.

Summary Statistics

Statistics cover the 86 scheduled presenters (keynote speakers excluded). Gender is inferred from first names and is approximate; ambiguous names are counted as “Other/undetermined”. Presenters with a joint policy and academic affiliation are counted under Policy. For the theme chart, papers are counted under their session’s major theme, except five fiscal-policy papers scheduled in other sessions, which are counted under fiscal policy.

Presenters by country of institution: Australia (32), Japan (22), South Korea (6), United Arab Emirates (5), Singapore (5), Hong Kong (3), Malaysia (2), New Zealand (2), China (2), Ireland (1), Denmark (1), Macao (1), United States of America (1), Belgium (1), Taiwan (1); no institutional affiliation (1, not shown on the map).
